scenario_stem:
Kestrel Bay Fisheries is a fishing business based in Country X that employs 18 crew members across 3 boats. It catches about 12 tonnes of sardines a month and sells them fresh to a wholesale fish merchant at $3 per kilogram. The business has made a small profit for 6 years, but rising fuel costs are squeezing margins.

The owner, Marta Ilves, is considering spending $120,000 on a small canning plant to process sardines into tinned fish sold at $7 per kilogram, with $2 of extra running costs per kilogram. A bank has offered a loan for the equipment, but the wholesale merchant has promised a 10% price rise if Kestrel Bay signs a fresh 2-year supply contract instead. She also estimates the plant would need 6 extra workers once running.

Way 2: Improving presentation and branding [k], by relabelling tins as Kestrel Bay sardines with attractive packaging so the business can charge more than unbranded fresh fish [app].

The family is considering installing cheese and yogurt equipment costing $95,000 so the surplus and part of the remaining output can be made into processed products bringing in $1.40 per litre-equivalent. A rival farm locally has just started selling yogurt, and the processor has hinted that the raw-milk price may be cut by 8% next year. The family also plans to supply 4 local shops and 2 cafés directly, replacing some raw-milk sales over time.

The owners must decide between two options. Option one is to spend $1.5 million on new rolling machinery to make higher-value finished sections for export, possibly aided by government grants of up to $400,000 that require at least 200 jobs to be kept. scenario_stem:

The owner, Jonas Lindqvist, is considering building a sawmill and planing facility costing $700,000 to turn logs into planks sold at $210 per tonne. A neighbouring sawmill has offered a fixed three-year contract for Pinecrest's logs instead. Planks for construction must meet strict quality standards. scenario_stem:
Ashford Grain Co-operative is a primary sector partnership of 14 wheat farmers in Country X, farming 2,300 hectares together and selling 9,000 tonnes of wheat a year to exporters at $240 per tonne. Country X is industrialising fast: manufacturing grew by 8.2% last year, and domestic bakeries and pasta makers now import $30 million of flour annually.

The farmers are considering a $500,000 co-operative flour mill to supply domestic bakeries; flour sells at $360 per tonne, keeping $120 per tonne of added value within the group. The alternative is to continue the exporters' long-standing contracts. The mill would need government approval and a trained miller, and the group currently employs 45 seasonal workers at harvest time. The mill would run in 2 shifts to supply the bakeries year-round.

questions.question_text: Outline why the primary sector's share of employment falls as a country develops.
questions.model_answer: As incomes rise, spending shifts from farm output towards manufactured goods and services; mechanisation and capital equipment replace farm workers, and higher wages in secondary and tertiary activities pull labour out of agriculture [2].
